Inaki,

Thank you for the response.

I did something a bit different and got it to work.

My final two questions for now, is the output from my temp%>%run(until=sim_time)  statement lists each subsystem failure with a value attached to each subsystem in ascending order. For example, the first "brakes failure" reads as brakes0 and the second reads as brakes1, so on and so forth.

1) Is there a function within simmer to group all failures for each subsystem to analyze things such as: Average activity time, crew delay time, etc?

2) The simulation below is for one 20 year simulation. If I want to replicate this say, 2000 times, do you have a recommendation to do this efficiently. I tried rollback, but I suspect I am placing it in the wrong place.

Thanks so much for you input. Simmer is a great tool!

The working output is below the code for a single simulation

**Repairable Systems Simulation Tool: Subsystem Level**
=======================================================

```{r}
repair_sim_subs <- function(xxx,temp,sss,sim_time){

library(simmer)      ##Call Simmer Library
library(simmer.plot) ##Call Simmer Plot Library
library(gdata)       ##Call gdata Library
library(poisson)     ##Call poisson Library
library(parallel)
library(hms)
set.seed(sss)        #Set a random seed for this simulation

require(gdata)

i<- 1
sim_input <-read.xls ((xxx), sheet = 1, header = TRUE) #Read in Repairable System Spreadsheet

while(i < length(sim_input$subsystem)+1){
rep1   <- sim_input[i,4]       ##Repair distribution parameter 1
rep2   <- sim_input[i,5]       ##Repair distribution parameter 2
delay1 <- sim_input[i,15]      ##Delay distribution parameter 1
delay2 <- sim_input[i,16]      ##Delay distribution parameter 2

temp <- simmer()               ##Instantiate the environment

assign(paste0(sim_input[i,1]),           ##Unique Trajectories for each Subsystem
sub_traj <-
  trajectory(name="Subsystem's Path")%>%

  log_("Subsystem has failed.")%>%

  timeout(function(){runif(1,delay1,delay2)})%>%

  log_("Crew Arrives.")%>%

  set_attribute("Fail_time",function(){now(temp)})%>%
  seize("counter")%>%
  log_(function() {paste("Begin Repair")})%>%
  timeout(function(){runif(1,rep1,rep2)})%>%
  release("counter")%>%
  log_(function(){paste("Repaired")}),sub_traj,.GlobalEnv)
i<-i+1
}

sim_input <- assign("sim_input",sim_input,.GlobalEnv)     ##Call Excel Sheet into Trajectories

 temp <-simmer("System")%>% add_resource("counter",preemptive = TRUE)       ##Design the system

 for(i in 1:length(sim_input$subsystem)){

   ##
intensity <- function(t) (sim_input[ i ,3]/sim_input[ i ,2])*((t/sim_input[ i ,2])^sim_input[ i ,3]-1)
rate <- rweibull(sim_input[ i ,2],sim_input[ i ,3])
num.events <- 1000
keep<-nhpp.sim(rate, num.events, prob.func=intensity)

   if(length(keep[which((keep<sim_time)&(keep>0))])<1){

  print(paste("No",sim_input[i,1], "Failures"))
}

else{
  temp <- temp %>% add_generator(as.character(sim_input[ i ,1]),get(as.character(sim_input[ i ,1])),at(keep[which((keep<sim_time)&(keep>0))]))}

 }

  temp%>%run(until=1000)                              ##Run the System

  print(temp%>%                                       ##Summary Statistics for the System
  get_mon_arrivals)

plot(sub_traj)
}

#######
repair_sim_subs("simmerinput.xls",temp,sample(1:1000000,1),20)
#######

```

bankModel <- function(input)
{
  customer <- trajectory("Customer's path") %>%
    log_("Here I am") %>%
    timeout(10) %>%
    log_("I must leave")

  bank <- simmer("bank") %>%
    add_generator("Customer", customer, at(1:input$customers)) %>%
    run() %>%
    wrap()

messages.subject: Re: [simmer-devel] Re: Model Validation and testing
messages.body_plain:
Validation means different things in different contexts. In ML you're holding some data back to validate the model fit to the data. When doing DES you're constructing a model programmatically, a very different exercise than fitting. It's probably a fairly complicated model (unless you assume multivariate queuing theory to be simple). So what I do is for the first step is validate any known physical constraints of the system. For example, in a patient disease simulation -- do all trajectories die at most once? This is more similar to debugging than validation at this stage, but it's a great first step. Are there any constraints on the system must be satisfied. Spot auditing trajectories at random is an excellent exercise, making sure to pull at least one containing every possible event.

The next step is seeing if the parameters of the model be tweaked in such a way that grossly simplify the model to a known one. If so, run all these identified parameter sets simulations and compare with known simple models. For example, in disease simulation I turn off secular death from competing risks, and make the odds of all complications but one incredibly small. Then running the model, does the simulation reproduce the marginal rate and known distributions? I.e. can it reproduce a known simple model with restricted parameters? The general focus here is validating each parameter (or a minimal set of parameters) has the desired influence when everything that can be turned off is.

Next, are there published similar complex models that I can set the parameters to match? For example, in our upcoming paper we have 3 conditions we investigate as competing risks. A well known model already exists for one of the conditions, and it was constructed by a very different method. So we turn off the 2 conditions not published and run the model with the parameters from the published one and see if one can reproduce the results. For our case our model fortunately reproduced the published result and the manuscript is under minor revision at present.

understand, you don't want to stop the generators, but just to spit
arrivals at certain periods. Moreover, if you use one of these
convenience functions, you should *never* return -1, because the
convenience function will do it for you if it's required (functions

every=NULL).

generator <- from_to(0, 2, function() rexp(100, 1), arrive=FALSE, every=10)

interarrivals, exponentially distributed in this case, but does not
know a thing about the period. And yet, from_to manages to spit these
interarrivals between (0, 2), (10, 12), (20, 22), etc.

from_to(24, 48, function() sample(tuesday_data, ...), arrive=FALSE, every=168)
...

interarrival per call or a bunch of them: it doesn't matter, because
"from_to" will cut and insert a leap in the right place. In fact, it's
better to return many interarrival times per call for the sake of
performance.

general. Because what you get from that is not the original arrival
process, but a kind of decimation of the original.

> I then add on to this the first hour of
> the day, so for mondays this is 0, tuesdays this is 24, wednesdays is 48 etc
> etc.

You don't need to do that, because you are going to take differences.
Just add a zero at the beginning, always.

> Then my monday_data is calculated as diff(0,6,9,12,12,14,15,18) to give me
> an interarrival list time of 6,3,3,3,1,1,3.

I suppose you meant 6, 3, 3, 0, 2, 1, 3. As I said, it is ok to return
a zero, you don't need to add 0.01 or something like that.

> When I am passing the sample data straight in as a singular group of

> the lowest interarrivals first and progressing to higher interarrival times.

No, it's not. from_to takes the interarrivals and uses them in the
given order. Try it out yourself:

gen <- from_to(0, 24, function() c(6, 3, 3, 0, 2, 1, 3), arrive=FALSE,
every=168)
gen() # first week
#> [1] 6 3 3 0 2 1 3
gen() # second week
#> [1] 156   3   3   0   2   1   3

etc. As you can see, from_to returns exactly the interarrivals given.
It's just adding the appropriate lag between weeks.

> This was the reason originally I started passing through singular sample

return the diffs. That's all. The rest is handled by from_to.

> I tried cbinding the day of week function call, and if this was not the same

generator to the other". All the generators are active all time. They
just spit arrivals at the right time thanks to from_to.
